verdicts.reason: Both score the same observable trait -- repeated campaign slogans, mass-appeal language, and campaign metadata versus bespoke docket-specific prose -- with essentially interchangeable anchors.
A mass-campaign form letter is typically polished and standardized, so it would score high on campaign residue and low on unpolished grassroots voice.
Counting explicit CFR part/section citations is unrelated to whether the comment develops an argument that the statute fails to authorize the rule.
Y demands a named location, address, or stated distance from a facility, while X credits occupational or general direct exposure with no geographic specificity at all.
Both ask whether the comment sets out a concrete alternative regulatory design specific enough to implement, versus offering nothing.
Error-laden earnest personal prose and standardized coordinated-campaign language are near-opposite signals about the comment's origin.
A sustained first-person account of workplace or health exposure with no address or facility proximity scores high on Y and low on X's location-anchored scale.
A corporate or trade-association letterhead submission scores high on prestige wrapper but low on the specifically government/state template markers Y requires.
Y is about delegating substantive argument to another commenter's filing and explicitly caps mere coalition name-dropping at 5, which is exactly what X scores as maximal density.
X credits concrete local consequences even when stated impersonally, whereas Y requires a sustained first-person stake narrative, so a geographically specific but impersonal comment splits the two.
Talking about process mechanics and extension requests is a distinct behavior from parroting the proposed rule's own summary text back as commentary.
Both score the identical construct -- OCR substitution errors, split words, glyph codes, RECEIVED/POSTMARKED stamps, and fax header junk indicating a paper-route submission.
Both score extraction and filing debris in the text -- OCR corruption, duplicated headers/covers, page or slide fragments, and attachment references -- against clean native prose.

X requires the citations be weakly integrated or decorative and scores 0 when every citation is tightly tied to a claim, while Y scores high on sheer accumulation of statistics regardless of integration quality.

X keys on document-level prestige packaging (letterhead, senior signatory) while Y keys on asserted scale and standing (member counts, reach, longevity), and a plain-text comment claiming 50,000 members splits them.
Emotional intensity of register is independent of whether the commenter describes their own operational practice in the regulated activity.

Y additionally requires the writer be an unrepresented private individual and scores 0 for institutional plural voice, so an owner or officer narrating first-hand exposure on behalf of an entity scores high on X and low on Y.
Both score whether the comment supplies its own derived monetary compliance-cost figures with the basis stated, versus no figures.
